name: Crayon Cartoon
basis: why: wobbly outline, unmixed box colours, one-direction fill that skips; how: crayon palette, streak fills leaving paper, outline last

lumenary.blurb: A page from a picture book: thick wobbly outlines, a few bright colours from the crayon box, and waxy strokes that never quite fill the shape.

facts.bestOn: Simple subjects: a pet, a house, a face

why: A crayon drawing has rules of its own. The outline comes first and it wobbles. Colours come straight from the box, with no mixing. The filling is done in one direction, misses the corners, and lets the paper sparkle through wherever the wax skipped. It is the opposite of polish, and it is immediately warm.
how: Reduce the picture to a few simple shapes.
Swap each colour for the nearest crayon in a box of sixteen.
Push every shape about with slow noise so that no edge is straight.
Fill each colour with streaks in one direction, leaving paper where the wax skipped.
Lift the crayon before the outline, leaving a pale gap.
Draw the thick dark outline last.
history: Wax crayons became a school staple after 1903, when Binney and Smith in Pennsylvania began selling boxes of eight colours for a nickel. Coloured chalks and pastels are far older, but the wax stick was clean, cheap and safe for small children. Illustrators have long borrowed the look for picture books, because a crayon line tells a child that this is something they could draw too.
terms: The roughness of paper that catches crayon, chalk or pencil.
How much of the paper a medium actually hides.
Giving each pixel the most common value among its neighbours, which removes specks.
paragraphs: The picture is reduced to a few simple shapes, and each shape’s colour is swapped for the nearest crayon in a box of sixteen after being made more vivid. Two shapes that land on the same crayon are treated as one, with no outline between them. Nothing drawn by a small hand is straight, so every shape is pushed about before drawing: each pixel looks up its shape at a position shifted by slow value noise. Outlines are the boundaries of the shifted shapes, thickened.

Crayon is wax dragged over rough paper. Each colour is given one stroke direction, and the pixel’s coordinates are rotated into it. A noise stretched about nineteen times longer along the stroke than across it gives the streaks. A second, fine noise is the tooth of the paper. Wax lands where the sum of the two clears a threshold that the pressure slider lowers, so light pressure leaves paper showing in the hollows. Close to an outline the coverage is cut by about half, because a child lifts the crayon before reaching the line.

equations.tex: u=x\cos a+y\sin a,\qquad v=-x\sin a+y\cos a,\qquad a=\pi\cdot\operatorname{hash}(\text{colour})
equations.note: Coordinates along (u) and across (v) the stroke direction of one colour.
How much wax lands: N is value noise, w the pressure slider (0.1 to 1).
The wobble: shapes are read at a position displaced by up to A pixels.

presets.text: Light pressure on sugar paper leaves most of the page showing.
Bright crayons on black paper glow.
The picture’s own colours with little wobble make a tidier drawing.
